## *Revenons à nos moutons*

::: {.claimcard}
"The expected change in [unit quantity] among [target population] for a 1-percentage-point difference in unemployment, holding [assumptions] fixed."
:::

::: {.small}
- Unit quantity – a *person's* cosmopolitan framing, or a *country-year* mean?
- Target population – which countries, which years?
:::

::: {.fragment}
**In chat, now:** your one-sentence estimand for the claim. Type it, hold it, send on "go".
:::

::: notes
Back to our own paper, then, with the template from Lundberg and colleagues in hand, and this one is a chat exercise. Write the statement on the slide with the brackets filled in: your one-sentence estimand for the claim. Type it, hold it, send when I say go. [go; read three or four aloud.] Look at the spread in the chat – some of you wrote about a person's framing, some about a country-year average, some named different years. None of those are wrong. They are different questions, with different confounding stories, and the coefficient means something different in each. That spread, in a class that has just followed the same slides, is the same kind of disagreement that the five free-phase analyses of our paper showed. Keep your statement, because it goes into your preregistration in Task 5, and when we reach the menu of choices you will also see what the choice of unit did to the estimates of the five analysts.
:::

## Causal identification in this design {#we-cannot-identify-a-causal-effect-here .smaller}

::: {.small}
Observational panel · 27 countries · no assignment mechanism · feedback between the variables · a decade of shared shocks.

Nothing in this design licenses "unemployment **causes** a shift in EU framing".
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
So why draw a causal graph at all?
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Because the graph still does three jobs that do not need identification:

- It says **which association** you are after – for instance the total effect, rather than whatever the software returns
- It tells you **which variables belong in the model**, and, just as usefully, which do not
- It makes your assumptions **legible and arguable** – a reader can disagree with an arrow, and that is a productive disagreement
:::

::: notes
The template you have just filled in speaks of an expected change in framing for a one-percentage-point difference in unemployment, which sounds causal, so it is worth being plain about what this design can deliver. This is an observational panel of twenty-seven countries. Nobody assigned unemployment to anyone. The variables plausibly feed back into each other over time, and the whole decade is shot through with shocks that hit everybody at once. Nothing in that design licenses the sentence "unemployment causes a shift in EU framing". [advance] So why draw a causal graph at all? [advance] Because the graph does three jobs that do not need identification. It says which association you are actually after – the total effect, say, rather than whatever the software happens to return. It tells you which variables belong in your model, and just as usefully which do not. And it makes your assumptions explicit, so that a reader can disagree with a specific arrow, which is a more productive argument to have than one about a coefficient.
:::

## Publishing the estimand and the graph {#say-it-in-public-or-it-does-not-count .smaller}

::: {.small}
The graph and the estimand are only worth anything if they are **published where someone else can read them**:

- in the paper itself
- **before** the model runs, not reconstructed afterwards
- with the **limitations named by you** before a reviewer finds them
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
In Task 5 you enter all of that in a block of the report in your workspace – the estimand, the graph-based justification, the one specification, and the rule for what would count as support – and you do it **before** you run the model.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The technical name for that is preregistration, and it fixes the question before anyone knows the result.
:::

::: notes
One more step follows from this, and it is where the tasks are heading. A graph you drew and did not publish is worth almost nothing. It has to be written down in the paper, where someone else can read it. It has to be written before the model runs, not reconstructed afterwards once you know which way the coefficient went, because a graph drawn after the fact will very reliably justify the result you already have. And you have to name the limitations yourself, before a reviewer finds them. [advance] In Task 5 you will enter all of that in a block of the report in your workspace: your estimand, your graph-based justification, the one specification you will run, and your rule for what would count as support – and you will do it before you run the model. [advance] The technical name for that is preregistration.
:::
## The EU-frames DAG, half built

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}

```{r}
#| label: teney-dag
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 5.8
# ggdag rendering of the starter DAG for Task 2. This reproduces the EXACT
# graph in _workspaces/eu-frames/R/dag_starter.R: the causal path of interest and the two
# confounder pairs (country, year) are drawn SOLID; the three arguable nodes
# (growth, bailout, politicisation) are present but UNCONNECTED – the edges
# that participants decide whether to add in Task 2. That is what makes it
# 'half built'. Nodes are coloured by ROLE (predictor orange, outcome navy,
# candidates light grey), labels sit inside the nodes in white/dark, edges are
# thick and gently curved.
dag <- ggdag::dagify(
  framing ~ unemployment,
  framing ~ country + year,
  unemployment ~ country + year,
  exposure = "unemployment",
  outcome  = "framing",
  coords = list(
    x = c(unemployment = 0, framing = 3, country = 1, year = 2),
    y = c(unemployment = 0, framing = 0, country = 1.4, year = 1.4)))

# dagify() has no way to hold a node with no edges, so the three candidates
# join the picture at the tidy-data layer instead. 'growth' is nudged down off
# the year -> unemployment crossing arrow; the other two are kept clear of the
# committed edges.
candidates <- tibble::tribble(
  ~name,             ~x,    ~y,
  "growth",           0.9, -1.0,
  "bailout",          1.5, -1.2,
  "politicisation",   3.0, -0.95)

# Role lookup → drives node fill and label colour; short display labels keep
# the longer names from overflowing the nodes (the underlying graph keeps the
# full names, matching dag_starter.R).
roles <- tibble::tibble(
  name = c("unemployment", "framing", "country", "year",
           "growth", "bailout", "politicisation"),
  role = c("predictor", "outcome", "adjusted", "adjusted",
           "candidate", "candidate", "candidate"),
  disp = c("unemp.", "framing", "country", "year",
           "growth", "bailout", "politic."))
role_fill <- c(predictor = orange, outcome = ncl_blue,
               adjusted = "#c7ccd2", candidate = "#dde2e7")
# White labels read on the dark predictor/outcome fills; navy on the light greys.
role_lab  <- c(predictor = "#FFFFFF", outcome = "#FFFFFF",
               adjusted = ncl_blue, candidate = "#5d666e")

dag_tidy <- ggdag::tidy_dagitty(dag)
ggdag::update_dag_data(dag_tidy) <- ggdag::pull_dag_data(dag_tidy) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows(candidates) |>
  dplyr::left_join(roles, by = "name") |>
  dplyr::mutate(role = factor(role,
    levels = c("predictor", "outcome", "adjusted", "candidate")))

ggplot2::ggplot(dag_tidy,
    ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend)) +
  # geom_dag_edges_arc() takes `arrow`, not the `arrow_directed` of
  # geom_dag_edges(); and the nodes are wide enough to paint over an arrowhead,
  # so end_cap stops each edge short of the circle it points at.
  ggdag::geom_dag_edges_arc(curvature = 0.18, edge_colour = grey_mid,
                            edge_width = 1.1,
                            end_cap = ggraph::circle(11, "mm"),
                            arrow = grid::arrow(
                              length = grid::unit(9, "pt"), type = "closed")) +
  ggdag::geom_dag_point(ggplot2::aes(fill = role), shape = 21,
                        size = 32, stroke = 0, colour = "white") +
  ggdag::geom_dag_text(ggplot2::aes(label = disp, colour = role),
                       size = 5.2, fontface = "bold") +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = role_fill, guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = role_lab, guide = "none") +
  ggdag::theme_dag() +
  ggplot2::expand_limits(x = c(-0.7, 3.7), y = c(-1.9, 2.1)) +
  ggplot2::theme(plot.margin = ggplot2::margin(14, 14, 14, 14))
```

::: {.dagcode}
The same graph in R. Every arrow is a formula, read outcome-first – so a `#` takes an arrow out and the code still runs:
:::

```r
ggdag::dagify(
  framing ~ unemployment,
  framing ~ country + year,
  unemployment ~ country + year,
  # framing ~ growth,        # uncomment the
  # unemployment ~ growth,   # arrows you believe
  exposure = "unemployment", outcome = "framing"
) |> dagitty::adjustmentSets()
```
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.small}
- Drawn: the path of interest and two confounders, **country and year**, which two-way fixed effects adjust for
- Not yet wired: growth (confounder?) · bailout (mediator?) · politicisation (mediator?)
- Your part: add the edges you believe, then run `adjustmentSets()`
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
This is the graph that you will finish yourselves. The solid part is what we are committing to: unemployment to framing is the path of interest, and country and year are the two confounders – stable national traits on one side, EU-wide shocks in a given year on the other. Run `adjustmentSets()` on this graph and it returns country and year, which is what a two-way fixed-effects model absorbs. So the graph and the baseline model make the same claim, once as a picture and once as a regression. The three pale nodes are yours to wire up, and they are genuine decisions. Is GDP growth a time-varying confounder that fixed effects cannot reach – a slump that raises unemployment and sours sentiment in the same year? Is the bailout a mediator, in which case you leave it alone if you want the total effect? Multi100 told us to disregard politicisation – was that defensible? The code beside the picture is the same graph written as R formulas, one arrow to a line, so wiring a node up means uncommenting the line you believe and running it again to see what the adjustment set has become. You do that in Hands-on 2, and the adjustment set you settle on there decides the model that you carry into the menu and into your preregistration.
:::
